claims.explanation: Selectivity of the HDAC inhibitor JNJ-26481585 is best explained by intact p53 signaling and dependence on class I HDAC activity, particularly HDAC1/2, which are required for the transcriptional response to DNA damage and apoptosis. Lines with TP53 mutations or defects in p53 pathway (e.g., MDM2 amplification, CDKN2A loss) are less sensitive, while those with high HDAC1/2 expression or specific oncogenic drivers such as BRAF and EGFR may be more sensitive due to oncogene addiction and reliance on HDAC-mediated survival pathways.

features.basis: TP53 mutations are enriched in least affected lines and rare in most sensitive lines; p53 is required for HDAC inhibitor-induced apoptosis.
JNJ-26481585 is a class I HDAC inhibitor with prolonged inhibition of HDAC1; high expression may predict response.
Class I HDACs including HDAC2 are primary targets; high expression may increase dependence.
BRAF mutations appear in several sensitive melanoma and colorectal lines; oncogenic BRAF may confer HDAC inhibitor sensitivity.
EGFR mutations are present in sensitive lung and esophageal lines; EGFR signaling may sensitize to HDAC inhibition.
MDM2 is a listed target and can inhibit p53; overexpression may reduce sensitivity to HDAC inhibitor-induced apoptosis.
CDKN2A loss appears in some resistant lines and may impair cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.
PTEN mutations are common in sensitive lines (melanoma, kidney, thyroid); loss may increase dependence on HDAC-mediated survival.
ATM mutations appear in several sensitive lines; defective DNA damage response may enhance sensitivity to HDAC inhibitors.
ARID1A mutations are present in multiple sensitive lines; chromatin remodeling defects may increase HDAC dependence.
KMT2D mutations appear in several sensitive lines; altered histone methylation may synergize with HDAC inhibition.
EP300 mutations are seen in sensitive lines; loss of histone acetyltransferase may increase reliance on HDAC activity.
